newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - W.CAPE REWRITES BUDGET RULES - BY T.TWINE.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - W.CAPE REWRITES BUDGET RULES - BY T.TWINE.

text.p: By Tony Twine, an economist at Econometrix financial consultancy

Given the consummate ease with which the provincial government of the Western Cape has "balanced" its 1997/98 budget, simply by massaging the conventional definitions of a few concepts, no politician ever again has to wrestle over niceties such as whether budgeted expenditure is covered by budgeted income.

The solution, it turns out, is so simple that it is a wonder of the modern age that budgetary deficits could have caused such a problem between the Republicans and Democrats for all these years. One can only hope that President Clinton is not so totally immersed in his Middle East discussions that he misses the subtle genius of the new technique that would, if applied to the United States federal budget, allow it to be balanced not by the year 2000, but by tomorrow.

The skeleton of the problem and the recently devised solution to it, are as follows. South Africa has one national government (this is in itself a useful concept), with nine second tier provincial governments. Seven of the nine provincial governments have ANC majorities in their legislatures - the Western Cape has a National Party (remember them?) legislative majority, while KwaZulu Natal is in the hands of the IFP. Together with Gauteng, the industrial hub of the country, they account for more than two-thirds of the country's GDP.
Reportedly growing faster than any of the other provinces, the Western Cape is, therefore, both politically and economically important.

Second tier governments (as well as the third tier local authorites) are not supposed to run budgetary deficits on current expenditure. The provincial Borrowing Act lays down the rules for any borrowing that may take place, restricting it to the financing of capital projects under the massive provisor that the means of repayment must be clearly spelled out when any borrowing is undertaken.

The provinces are also highly restricted in terms of raising their own internal fiscal revenue. Motor vehicle licence fees, entertainment and gambling taxes and charges for certain services (e.g. hospitals), as well as cross-border charges for services rendered to other provinces, make up the rather scanty list of potential revenue sources outside of central government funding. In the case of the Western Cape 91 percent of the 1997/98 revenue will come from central government.

The way that the central government allocates its block payments to each of the provinces is via the Financial and Fiscal Committee (FFC). Each province presents its spending requirements, and these are then panel-beaten into shares of the total available allocation from the national budget. Inevitably, the whole is usually smaller than the sum of the provincial demands for spending powers. The provinces then have to rework their spending priorities in the light of having less income than they might have initially budgeted for.

That is exactly what happened to the provinces for the 1997/98 fiscal year, and the Western Cape found itself with some 780 million rand less income than it had originally planned for. This equated to about seven percent of the original income and expenditure budgets, which, you will remember, are supposed to be in strict balance. Legally the province is not allowed to borrow to cover current expenditure, and without much leeway to increase its own limited revenue, the provincial government was forced to revise its spending priorities. Not all those priorities were flexible - for instance, increases (some 80 million rand) in pension payments were decided at national government level.

The provincial administration, to use their own phraseology, had already trimmed away fat in the budget, and was forced to cut not only into the meat, but into the bone itself of its spending programmes. Needless to say, these metaphors sent the local media into a gory carnivorous feeding-frenzy.

The reworking of the budgeted expenditure produced savings of 620 million rand, or a net 540 million rand after the adjustment for pensions. Even Karl Marx would have recognised that these savings were 240 million rand short of the mark. Appropriately scaled up, this apparent deficit could have drawn the wrath of the U.S. congress down on the head any presidential administration.

Apparent deficit? It is all smoke and mirrors, say the members of the Western Cape provincial executive. It is not really a deficit at all, they say, it is just that there is no specific plan available at the beginning of the budgetary period to close the gap between income and expenditure. When is a fiscal deficit not a fiscal deficit? Clearly it is not one whenever the provincial fiscus is content to budget on a manna from heaven basis, even if the manna has to take the form of a lump sum payment from national government just before the end of the fiscal year. But the manna budgeting principal can easily contribute to a delay in reaching the land of milk and honey - does South Africa have another 40 years to wander around in the fiscal desert? Probably not.

John Keynes, Harold Wilson and Bill Clinton, eat your hearts out. Why did you not think of not having to finance deficit budgets simply by assuming that either or both of your income and expenditure estimates would be wrong? Mind you, this one budgeting style, albeit flawed, represents an advance from the National Party budgets of about a decade ago. In those days, it would have presented a budget of the required deficit size, and gone ahead and spent the money it wanted to with scant regard for budgeted spending constraints.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
